title: Distance Sampling for Aerial Waterbird Surveys—Application to an Ephemeral Wetland of International Significance
content:
ABSTRACT

Ephemeral wetlands can radically change the ecology of arid landscapes but are difficult to robustly survey when flooded, challenging conservation management. The Fortescue Marsh (Martuyitha) is one of the largest water features of northwest Australia, with significant cultural and ecological value. Our aim was to develop a repeatable aerial waterbird survey methodology allowing systematic counts across years with different flooding extents, and accounting for differences in species responsiveness to the aircraft (i.e., detectability). We carried out systematic helicopter surveys of the marsh, flying georeferenced 1-km-spaced transects to proportionally cover the entire flooded area. We estimated the distance to bird observations using markings on the aircarft windows, which were calibrated at regular intervals and accounting for aircraft flight height. Data demonstrated both an effect of transect strip width and position on raw waterbird counts and community composition, reflecting species differences in responsiveness to the aircraft. Detectability (p) for 15 waterbird species (average p = 0.79 ± 0.17), together with three other bird taxa, was positively correlated with group size and body mass. Distance sampling was used to estimate population sizes (N̂$$ \hat{N} $$), which were strongly correlated with maximum counts for each of 15 waterbird species (p < 0.001), but averaged 1.45 times greater than maximum counts recorded for these species. Significant differences in waterbird counts and community composition due to transect width and position undermine confidence in interpretation of raw counts, highlighting the importance of carrying out statistical correction for species' detectability. We present a practical, field-ready approach to carrying out data collection suitable for Distance sampling analysis.
